Hammanskraal | The Aftermath

By: Masa Kekana | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Now that the cameras, mics and blue lights have left the streets of Hammanskraal, the residents are left grieving the untimely deaths of their loved ones, while still living with the deadly weapon; th

Unique Selling Point:
The May madness of preventable deaths due to cholera in Hammaskraal sent shock waves around the country when dozens of people perished. It rightfully grabbed the attention of the President, senior politicians and the media. But as is the case with most breaking news in SA (and globally), we move on and the victims are left behind.

What is life like living in an area where you could die from the very source of life? The problem has not gone away and the promises to resolve the problem remain empty. Hammanskraals water crises has existed since at least 2005. Some residents date their water woes in the area as far back as pre 1994. It was in 2019 when the Human Rights Commission released their findings on the poor state of the water affairs for Hammanskraal residents, and ever since then the coalition governments have not been able to get it together to solve a problem that had been in existence before coalition governments took over. What we saw following the deaths and as the numbers climbed, were politicians and different spheres of government pointing fingers at one another and no one wanting to take accountability for the unnecessary and preventable loss of lives.

But why was the water deadly in that one week? Where was it coming from? We were able to trace where the water source is.


Summary:
Hammanskraal has been a ticking time bomb for too many years. Government ignored the big bold red writing on the wall and we ended up making international news for deaths over something so preventable. At least 24 people died when they drank the water, not from the tap, but from the trucks that the municipality pays to deliver clean, safe drinking water. People of Hammanskraal have been living with deadly tap water for so long that they are so well trained to not drink that tap water. They even know how to use the deadly tap water without ingesting it. So they live with it, touch it, use it, but know not to drink it. They use it daily to even brush their teeth knowing not to make the mistake of consuming it. Intimately contacting the weapon that killed their loved ones. How does one live with such tragedy?

We meet the families left behind the ones who lost their lives. These are sons, daughters, mothers, fathers, nieces, nephews, aunts and uncles who have lost their lives abruptly and tragically. They were not just numbers but people who had dreams, personalities and loved ones.

This piece is to focus on the human element. Telling the stories of those who died, naming them and illustrating what life is like post the deaths but still having the fear lurking. It has been two months and there has been no resolution. The water is still contaminated, and locals are reliant on unreliable water trucks that also carried the water that killed people. It is a sad state of affairs for those left behind.

-Case studies
Lucas (26 years old) lost his mother who was in her forties and the bread winner. He now is raising his three younger siblings, two in primary school and one in high school. He is unemployed and has been terribly affected by the loss of his mother.

Mme Anna – Lost her husband of 25 years. He had just started a new job they were proud of, she is left to raise their three young children alone. She too is unemployed. It is more than the financial loss of losing the breadwinner for these cases studies, Mme Anna lost her first love and her best friend.

Ontatile – 23 years old and lost her mother who was in her forties. She is a single mother and also unemployed. She was with her mom when she started getting sick and waited for the ambulance with her. Ill treated by the hospital and not allowed to see her mother. She now raises her toddler and 12 year old sibling alone, with the help of her unemployed grandmother who does not live with them.

Moafrica wa Moila – He is the advocate representing the families in a class action law suit against the government. He also is born and bred in Hammanskraal and still has a home there. He is more of an expert and knowledgeable on the history.

-Interviews
Tshwane Mayor Cillers Brink. He this week said that local government not receiving co operation of the premier and announced that affected families would be compensated R30K.

Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi – To speak from provincial government stance, seeing as province has the powers to intervene and help.



Further information:
TREATMENT

Human interest and putting a face to the victims of these preventable deaths.
Drone shots of quiet Hammanskraal. The cold conditions with everyone indoors will illustrate the emptiness of the streets following the noise that was in the early days of the cholera outbreak.

So as we speak, we still haven't determined in cooperation with the Department of Health, Water and Sanitation where this came from.

UPSOUND: MASA: HOW DO WE KNOW THIS WON'T HAPPEN AGAIN?

UPSOUND MASA: Including your party
UPSOUND: Yes, I include my political party. Several promises were made, not just here but by other spheres of government.
VO 24: While Brink says the City has in the past four months allocated nearly half a billion rand to fix the water treatment plants in Hammanskraal, Advocate Moila has heard enough excuses and promises. He’s heading to court.
VIZ LAWYER
ADVOCATE UPSOUND: we wouldn't take the story that says we tested the water in Tshwane and there is no cholera. So therefore we don't know whether cholera comes from, it's not us. VO 25: But the people can’t wait…they’re still being delivered …handling, using…the very same water that may very well have killed their loved ones.
UPSOUND GEORGE: I’m really scared of the water, even if they say it's safe I just don't trust it anymore, I don't want to use it.
George Clip: 08:55 - 09:02
UPSOUND: ALETTAH: I’m scared of the water

UPSOUND ADVOCATE But we are working hard to find our own ways we do it ourselves. I have personally fundraised for three boreholes.
VO 27: It may not be the best solution, but some residents feel they have been left with no choice after decades of empty promises…

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Now that the cameras, mics and blue lights have left the streets of Hammanskraal, the residents are left grieving the untimely deaths of their loved ones, while still living with the deadly weapon; th
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The May madness of preventable deaths due to cholera in Hammaskraal sent shock waves around the country when dozens of people perished. It rightfully grabbed the attention of the President, senior politicians and the media. But as is the case with most breaking news in SA (and globally), we move on and the victims are left behind. What is life like living in an area where you could die from the very source of life? The problem has not gone away and the promises to resolve the problem remain empty. Hammanskraals water crises has existed since at least 2005. Some residents date their water woes in the area as far back as pre 1994. It was in 2019 when the Human Rights Commission released their findings on the poor state of the water affairs for Hammanskraal residents, and ever since then the coalition governments have not been able to get it together to solve a problem that had been in existence before coalition governments took over. What we saw following the deaths and as the numbers climbed, were politicians and different spheres of government pointing fingers at one another and no one wanting to take accountability for the unnecessary and preventable loss of lives. But why was the water deadly in that one week? Where was it coming from? We were able to trace where the water source is.
metadata.Summary: Hammanskraal has been a ticking time bomb for too many years. Government ignored the big bold red writing on the wall and we ended up making international news for deaths over something so preventable. At least 24 people died when they drank the water, not from the tap, but from the trucks that the municipality pays to deliver clean, safe drinking water. People of Hammanskraal have been living with deadly tap water for so long that they are so well trained to not drink that tap water. They even know how to use the deadly tap water without ingesting it. So they live with it, touch it, use it, but know not to drink it. They use it daily to even brush their teeth knowing not to make the mistake of consuming it. Intimately contacting the weapon that killed their loved ones. How does one live with such tragedy? We meet the families left behind the ones who lost their lives. These are sons, daughters, mothers, fathers, nieces, nephews, aunts and uncles who have lost their lives abruptly and tragically. They were not just numbers but people who had dreams, personalities and loved ones. This piece is to focus on the human element. Telling the stories of those who died, naming them and illustrating what life is like post the deaths but still having the fear lurking. It has been two months and there has been no resolution. The water is still contaminated, and locals are reliant on unreliable water trucks that also carried the water that killed people. It is a sad state of affairs for those left behind. -Case studies Lucas (26 years old) lost his mother who was in her forties and the bread winner. He now is raising his three younger siblings, two in primary school and one in high school. He is unemployed and has been terribly affected by the loss of his mother. Mme Anna – Lost her husband of 25 years. He had just started a new job they were proud of, she is left to raise their three young children alone. She too is unemployed. It is more than the financial loss of losing the breadwinner for these cases studies, Mme Anna lost her first love and her best friend. Ontatile – 23 years old and lost her mother who was in her forties. She is a single mother and also unemployed. She was with her mom when she started getting sick and waited for the ambulance with her. Ill treated by the hospital and not allowed to see her mother. She now raises her toddler and 12 year old sibling alone, with the help of her unemployed grandmother who does not live with them. Moafrica wa Moila – He is the advocate representing the families in a class action law suit against the government. He also is born and bred in Hammanskraal and still has a home there. He is more of an expert and knowledgeable on the history. -Interviews Tshwane Mayor Cillers Brink. He this week said that local government not receiving co operation of the premier and announced that affected families would be compensated R30K. Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi – To speak from provincial government stance, seeing as province has the powers to intervene and help.
metadata.Further information: TREATMENT Human interest and putting a face to the victims of these preventable deaths. Drone shots of quiet Hammanskraal. The cold conditions with everyone indoors will illustrate the emptiness of the streets following the noise that was in the early days of the cholera outbreak.
